_note:
Suspect counts are a ratchet, not a score: they may only stop growing. Two of these numbers are
explained rather than fixed, and both are recorded here because a number nobody can account for
gets --update'd blind.

(1) fil-PH 14: all fourteen are the same false positive -- a Han glossary term whose default is a
Latin brand name (B 站 -> "bilibili" 13 rows, 萌百 -> "Moegirlpedia" 1 row). That is the wording the
project intends to display in every locale that has no override: "bilibili" is the platform's own
name and appears in the English source string too. The rule fires because the term is Han and the
default is not Han, so it cannot tell "a translation leaked into this locale" from "the pinned
wording IS the brand name". Adding a fil-PH override equal to the default would satisfy the rule
while documenting nothing.

(2) ko-KR 31 (was 29): adding a 27th locale moves the cross-locale *median* length that the
length-outlier rule compares against, and two existing, untouched Korean rows crossed the 0.3x
threshold (eventsItems: 8 chars against a median of 21; costOnExceed: 7 against 20). Nothing in
ko-KR changed -- the median gained one more sample, and a length heuristic has no way to know that.


(3) th-TH 0. The first measured number for this locale was 13, and all thirteen were the same false
positive as fil-PH's above: the rule for a Han term whose default is a Latin brand name fires on rows
whose zh source does not even contain the term ("B 站" with a space in the dictionary against "B站"
without one in glossary.json), so any value carrying the Latin word "bilibili" matched. Measured on
the untouched id-ID locale: the same 13 rows, word for word. Rather than annotate a number that is
entirely noise, th-TH now carries an explicit override for every one of those terms -- which is also
the first time the file records "the Thai wording is the brand name" as a decision instead of leaving
it as an absence. The terms whose default is already Latin (bilibili / hololive / Tor / JSON / VTuber
...) still have no entry, and the note above says why.

(4) ko-KR stays 27 and no other locale moved: adding a 28th locale left the cross-locale median that
the length-outlier rule compares against unchanged for every key, so the rows that moved when the
27th locale arrived are back where they were before it. That 27 was a median shift, not a Korean
defect; both directions of the effect are worth the lines it takes to say so.

(5) Coverage denominator, same release: coverage.json moved 633 -> 638 for **every** locale (25 of
them changed), so no locale's own coverage changed -- the number of keys the UI uses grew by five
since the baseline was last written, and the tool counts each locale's own-provided keys, so the
denominator carried them along. Nothing in this change touched another locale's data.

(6) vi-VN 14, the 29th locale, measured after it landed: all fourteen are the same false positive as
fil-PH's item (1) -- a Han glossary term whose default is a Latin brand name (B 站 -> bilibili on 13 rows,
萌百 -> Moegirlpedia on 1). The pinned wording is the platform's own name and appears in the English source
string too, so it is the intended display, and the rule cannot tell "a translation leaked into this locale"
from "the pinned wording IS the brand name". vi-VN takes the Filipino convention rather than the Thai one
(the reasoning is recorded in glossary.json's _note_en: an entry only where the Vietnamese wording is not
the default), so those rows carry no override and the number is recorded rather than annotated away -- an
override equal to the default would satisfy the rule while documenting nothing, which is the note above
item (1) said about fil-PH.

Nothing else moved when this locale was added, and that was measured rather than assumed: the cross-locale
median the length-outlier rule compares against, the other 28 per-locale counts, and coverage.json's
per-locale numbers are all at their previous values (coverage 638/638 for every locale, unchanged). The
locale brought its own machine section and hand layer; no other locale's data was touched, which is why
there is no bisect to write here.
